name: Aquila
introduction: is the Eagle that carried Zeus’s thunderbolts. It flies along the Milky Way, and its brightest star, Altair, is one corner of the Summer Triangle. It straddles the celestial equator, so it can be seen from almost everywhere on Earth, best on northern summer evenings.

sections.title: What makes it special
paragraphs: [Altair](hip:97649), just 17 light-years away, spins so fast, once every nine hours or so, that it bulges strongly at its equator. In 2007, it became the first ordinary star besides the Sun whose surface was imaged in detail, revealing a cooler, darker equator and brighter poles.

Aquila also hides a giant. In 2024, the Gaia space telescope revealed [Gaia BH3](id:gaia-bh3), a dormant black hole about 33 times the mass of the Sun, betrayed only by the wobble of the old star that orbits it. Less than 2,000 light-years away, it is the most massive black hole of stellar origin known in our galaxy.

sections.title: Notable stars
paragraphs: Altair is flanked by [Tarazed](hip:97278) and [Alshain](hip:98036), forming a short, easy-to-spot line. Tarazed is an orange bright giant far in the background, while Alshain is a nearby yellow star only about 44 light-years away.

[Eta Aquilae](hip:97804) is one of the brightest Cepheid variables, pulsing in brightness every 7.2 days. Its variability was discovered in 1784 by Edward Pigott, a pioneer of variable-star astronomy. [Okab](hip:93747) and [Delta Aquilae](hip:95501) mark the eagle’s tail and wing.

sections.title: Beyond the stars
paragraphs: The reflection nebula [vdB 129](id:vdb-129) glows faintly in the eagle’s wing. In 1918, Nova Aquilae briefly became the brightest nova seen since Kepler’s supernova in 1604, nearly as bright as Sirius. Dark lanes of the Great Rift cross the Milky Way here, hiding the stars behind them.
